newTopics.title: How Animation Works: Frames and Motion
newTopics.summary: Animation is a trick of the eye: many still pictures shown quickly look like movement. Even a few frames can make a ball bounce or a horse gallop.
keyConcepts: Stop-motion: move it, photograph it, repeat
newTopics.tryIt: Make a flipbook on a stack of sticky notes: draw a ball on the last page, then move it a little higher on each page above. Flip from the back!

resources.title: Animal Locomotion, Volume IX: Horses
resources.creator: Eadweard Muybridge, 1887 (photogravures)
resources.note: Muybridge photographed movement frame by frame — an early step toward film and animation.

resources.title: Be an Animator
resources.note: Model a clay character, plan a storyboard and make a stop-motion film with a tablet or phone.

newTopics.title: Storyboards: Planning a Story in Pictures
newTopics.summary: Before a film or comic is made, artists sketch it as a row of small boxes. A storyboard shows what happens, where the 'camera' is, and how the story flows.
newTopics.tryIt: Draw a six-box storyboard of your morning, from waking up to leaving home. Use at least one close-up and one wide view.

newTopics.title: Digital Drawing and Creative Technology
newTopics.summary: Screens, code and sound can all be art tools. Digital artists experiment with GIFs, drawing machines and interactive pictures.
keyConcepts: Same design rules: shape, color, composition
newTopics.tryIt: Draw the same doodle three times, changing one small thing each time. Flip between them quickly — you've made a three-frame loop.
newTopics.imageNote: Most digital artworks are recent and protected by copyright, so this topic links to activities instead of showing pictures.
